title: First direct decoding of full words from the cortex of a paralyzed, anarthric man (UCSF, BRAVO trial)
summary: A speech neuroprosthesis built at the University of California, San Francisco, used deep-learning models to decode a paralyzed man's attempted speech at a median 15.2 words per minute.
account: A man had anarthria and severe spastic quadriparesis from an extensive pontine stroke at age 20. He is known in the press by the pseudonym Pancho. Before the study he typed about five words per minute with a head-controlled pointer. In February 2019, at the University of California, San Francisco, the 36-year-old man received a 128-electrode subdural electrocorticography array over sensorimotor cortex in the BRAVO trial (NCT03698149). Data collection began in April 2019. There were 50 sessions over 81 weeks at the participant's residence or a nearby office. Deep-learning models detected his attempted speech and classified words from a 50-word vocabulary. A natural-language model and a Viterbi decoder assembled sentences. On 15 July 2021 Moses and colleagues reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that he produced sentences at a median 15.2 words per minute with a median word error rate of 25.6%. The paper does not date the session in which this sentence decoding was achieved. In a letter to the journal on 13 October 2021, Michael J. Brenner of the University of Michigan Medical School asked whether the participant had anarthria or profound dysarthria, because his words "I am" are intelligible in the study video. On 8 November 2022 the same team reported that the participant spelled sentences by silent speech attempts from a vocabulary of 1,152 words, with stable signals beyond 128 weeks. The authors state that clinical and regulatory guidelines on the implanted connector kept him from using the system on his own.
purpose: Built to decode attempted speech into words and sentences for a person with anarthria. Restoring word-level communication was the intended benefit and is what occurred.
model_version: 128-electrode high-density ECoG array (16-by-8 lattice, 4 mm spacing); deep-learning speech-detection and word-classification models with natural-language model and Viterbi decoder; 50-word vocabulary

ratings.reason: One identifiable person gained the first decoding of his own full words, about three times faster than his pointer typing. The decoding was limited to a 50-word vocabulary in research sessions.

ai_role.statement: Deep-learning models detected attempted speech in 98% of attempts and classified words. A language model with Viterbi decoding assembled sentences. The output depended entirely on these models. Funding included a research contract under Facebook's Sponsored Academic Research Agreement. The paper states that no study hardware or data were transferred to any sponsor and that author disclosure forms are available at NEJM.org.

display.answer: The figures come from the makers' paper in the New England Journal of Medicine of 15 July 2021. The Advisory Board briefing and the Harvard Science in the News article report on the same study. Michael J. Brenner's letter of 13 October 2021 questions the diagnosis of anarthria. The follow-up of 8 November 2022 comes from the same team.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: A speech neuroprosthesis built at the University of California, San Francisco, used deep-learning models to decode a paralyzed man's attempted speech at a median 15.2 words per minute.
fields.account: A man had anarthria and severe spastic quadriparesis from an extensive pontine stroke at age 20. He is known in the press by the pseudonym Pancho. Before the study he typed about five words per minute with a head-controlled pointer. In February 2019, at the University of California, San Francisco, the 36-year-old man received a 128-electrode subdural electrocorticography array over sensorimotor cortex in the BRAVO trial (NCT03698149). Data collection began in April 2019. There were 50 sessions over 81 weeks at the participant's residence or a nearby office. Deep-learning models detected his attempted speech and classified words from a 50-word vocabulary. A natural-language model and a Viterbi decoder assembled sentences. On 15 July 2021 Moses and colleagues reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that he produced sentences at a median 15.2 words per minute with a median word error rate of 25.6%. The paper does not date the session in which this sentence decoding was achieved. In a letter to the journal on 13 October 2021, Michael J. Brenner of the University of Michigan Medical School asked whether the participant had anarthria or profound dysarthria, because his words "I am" are intelligible in the study video. On 8 November 2022 the same team reported that the participant spelled sentences by silent speech attempts from a vocabulary of 1,152 words, with stable signals beyond 128 weeks. The authors state that clinical and regulatory guidelines on the implanted connector kept him from using the system on his own.
